question: Article 21 of the Treaty on European Union sets out the principles and objectives which should guide the Union’s external action, including the promotion of democracy, the rule of law, human rights and respect for international law. Where the EU provides funding to Russian civil society organisations, human rights organisations and independent media, it is of essential importance that they adopt a genuine and unequivocal stance on Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. In this connection: 1.

Does the Commission require beneficiaries of EU funding to take an unequivocal stance on Russia’s aggression against Ukraine – recognising it as an illegal war of aggression by the Russian Federation – and to support Ukraine’s territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders, and does it verify their public statements in this regard?

Has the Commission identified any beneficiaries who, during the funding period, avoided unequivocally condemning the invasion, questioned Crimea’s status as part of Ukraine, opposed sanctions against Russia or arms supplies to Ukraine, or called for negotiations at the expense of Ukraine’s territorial integrity, and if so, what consequences have been brought to bear?

In the Commission’s view, is the provision of funding from EU public funds to an entity which does not explicitly oppose Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine compatible with Article 21 of the TEU and with the Union’s policy towards Ukraine?
answer: EN P-003335/2026 on behalf of the European Commission (3.11.2026) Since 2021, the EU has allocated EUR 70 million towards Russian civil society and independent media to protect fundamental rights and freedoms, promote a free and democratic Russia, and counter Kremlin narratives and hybrid threats.

The EU is committed to continue supporting the important work of Russian civil society organisations, human rights defenders and independent media and journalists inside and outside Russia. The EU delivers this support under conditions of severe repression.

Russian civil society activists, human right defenders and independent journalists continue to face persecution in the country and in exile, including threats to their own lives and that of their families. Public disclosure of entities receiving EU support would expose beneficiaries to important risks and is therefore not possible in the current context.

Accordingly, the Commission does not publicise the names of implementing partners to protect their ability to continue operating. The Commission receives regular and comprehensive reporting from beneficiaries and implementing partners to ensure that funding is properly accounted for. EU assistance is also subject to audit procedures to ensure proper use of funds and compliance with financial management rules.

The selection of project partners is aligned with the EU’s wartime approach to Russia, which focuses on supporting Ukraine, while also pursuing the isolation of Russia and supporting the work of Russian pro-democracy and anti-war civil society and independent media. Conditions for entities to receive support are determined in line with the EU’s Financial Regulation Article 38.

3(d)1 as well as EU values and priorities, including in the framework of the Thematic Programmes for Human Rights and Democracy2, and Civil Society Organisations3. Implementing partners are further required to guarantee full compliance with applicable sanctions policies, including at the level of final beneficiaries.
1 European Commission: Directorate-General for Budget, Financial regulation applicable to the general budget

of the Union (recast), Publications Office of the European Union, 2024, https://data.europa.eu/doi/10.2761/686790. 2 Multiannual Action Plan 2025-2027 for the Human Rights and Democracy Thematic Programme, 14 March 2025, https://international-partnerships.ec.europa.eu/document/download/4cc34cd1-dc34-461b-92a34e471fa0609a_en?filename=mip-2021-c2021-9620-human-rights-democracy-annex_en.pdf.
